\chapter{Why, Because, When}
\label{ch:ru-why-because-when}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask why and when in one word each, give a reason with potomu chto, put two things at the same moment with kogda, and write the comma Russian requires at the seam of every subordinate clause.}

The question family the book opened at poka closes here at five members -- kak, kakoy, chto, pochemu, kogda -- all one ancient stem, and two of them do double duty as joiners without changing a letter. potomu chto is pochemu with the question-stem swapped for the pointing-stem, so the answer is made out of the question. The chapter ends by stating the one Russian punctuation rule that has no exceptions, which is only sayable once the track owns the subordinators it applies to.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pachemú]{\ru{почему} — \textquotedblleft{}why,\textquotedblright{} which is really \textquotedblleft{}after what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:RU-C19-pochemu}



\begin{quote}
The two nursery words, and the newest mark on the page.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{мама}}, which is not inherited from anywhere — every language builds it out of the first sounds a baby makes
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{папа}}, and the rule that a word can wear a feminine ending and still be a man
  \item \emph{Recall:} the dash standing where the missing verb would be
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{я}} and \emph{\ru{ты}}, English \emph{thou}, and why \emph{\ru{вы}} is the safer one
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{почему}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{почему}} — \emph{pachemú} — \textbf{why}
\end{itemize}

Three syllables, stress right at the end: \emph{pa-che-MÚ}. It is the longest question word in this book and the easiest to take apart.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{почему}?} — on its own, it is a complete question.
\end{itemize}

One word, one rising voice, one mark at the end, and you have asked for a reason about anything that has just been said. That is worth having before you can give a reason yourself.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{почему}} is \textbf{\ru{по}} (\textquotedblleft{}after, along\textquotedblright{}) plus a case-form of \textbf{\ru{что}}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{по}} + \textbf{\ru{чему}} = \textbf{\ru{почему}} — literally, \emph{after what}
\end{itemize}

So the question family you opened in the last chapter has produced its third member: \textbf{\ru{как}}, \textbf{\ru{что}}, and now \textbf{\ru{почему}}. All three are the same ancient stem wearing different endings, and there are more still to come.

English does exactly the same trick and then forgets it did: \emph{wherefore} is \emph{for-what}, and \emph{therefore} is \emph{for-that}. Asking \emph{why} by asking \emph{after what} is not a Russian oddity — it is what most of Europe does.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{почему}} — \emph{pa-che-MÚ}, stress at the end
  \item it as a one-word question after anything you say
  \item the three of the family — \emph{\ru{как}, \ru{что}, \ru{почему}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}why.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{почему}}.) Which two pieces is it built from? (\textbf{\ru{по}} plus a form of \textbf{\ru{что}}.) What does it literally say? (\textbf{After what}.) And one look back: which word is built out of the first sounds a baby makes rather than inherited? (That is \textbf{\ru{мама}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[patamú shto]{\ru{потому} \ru{что} — the answer, made out of the question}

\label{lesson:RU-C19-potomu-chto}



\begin{quote}
The two formal parent-words, and yesterday's question.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{мать}}, straight from the root behind English \emph{mother}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{отец}}, which is \textbf{not} the father-root at all but a nursery word for \emph{daddy} that won
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{почему}}, and \emph{\ru{тоже}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{потому} \ru{что}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{потому} \ru{что}} — \emph{patamú shto} — \textbf{because}
\end{itemize}

Set the two words side by side and the shape gives itself away:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{почему}} — \emph{after \textbf{what}} — the question
  \item \textbf{\ru{потому}} — \emph{after \textbf{that}} — the answer
\end{itemize}

Russian answers \emph{why} by taking the same word, swapping the question-stem for the pointing-stem, and adding \textbf{\ru{что}} to hang the reason on. \textbf{\ru{почему}} asks; \textbf{\ru{по} \ru{тому}} points at the reason; \textbf{\ru{что}} carries the sentence that names it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — where the halves go, and where the comma goes}]
The thing that happened comes first; the reason follows:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{читаю}, \ru{потому} \ru{что} \ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{понимаю}} — \emph{ya ne chitáyu, patamú shto ya ne panimáyu} — I am not reading, \textbf{because} I do not understand.
\end{itemize}

The comma stands before \textbf{\ru{потому}}, not between \textbf{\ru{потому}} and \textbf{\ru{что}} — the two words are one joining word and nothing may come between them.

\textbf{\ru{и}} went bare; \textbf{\ru{но}} and \textbf{\ru{а}} each took a comma; this one takes a comma too. A shape is starting to show through those four, and the writing lesson at the end of this chapter is where it gets stated.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{читаю}, \ru{потому} \ru{что} \ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{понимаю}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{почему}?} and then answer yourself with \textbf{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}
  \item \emph{Build:} any sentence you own, a comma, \textbf{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}, and a reason
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}because.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}.) What is the one-word difference between it and \emph{why}? (\textbf{Question-stem} against \textbf{pointing-stem} — \emph{after what} against \emph{after that}.) Where does the comma go? (\textbf{Before \ru{потому}}, never inside the pair.) And one look back: which formal parent-word is really a nursery word that won? (That is \textbf{\ru{отец}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kagdá]{\ru{когда} — \textquotedblleft{}when,\textquotedblright{} and the family's fifth member}

\label{lesson:RU-C19-kogda-vopros}



\begin{quote}
Two things from the fridge, and the newest joining word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{молоко}}, on the root behind English \emph{milk}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{сыр}}, built on a word meaning \textbf{sour} — cheese named after what happens to the milk
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}, and \emph{\ru{один}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{меня} \ru{зовут}} — the they-form with nobody in it, and the object shape of \emph{\ru{я}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{когда}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{когда}} — \emph{kagdá} — \textbf{when}
\end{itemize}

Two syllables, stress on the second. Read the spelling and say the sound carefully, because they disagree again: the unstressed \textbf{\ru{о}} at the front says \emph{a}, exactly as it does in \textbf{\ru{один}}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{когда}?} — a complete question all by itself.
\end{itemize}

You now have three one-word questions: \textbf{\ru{что}?}, \textbf{\ru{почему}?} and \textbf{\ru{когда}?} — each of them a whole turn in a conversation, none of them needing a verb.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{когда}} is the same ancient question-stem as \textbf{\ru{как}}, \textbf{\ru{что}} and \textbf{\ru{почему}}, this time with an old time-ending welded on.

That makes four. Look at the front of each one and the family resemblance is on the page:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{как}} and \textbf{\ru{когда}} — both beginning with the same \textbf{\ru{к}}
  \item \textbf{\ru{что}} — the same stem, worn down further, which is why the letters no longer match
  \item \textbf{\ru{почему}} — the stem again, wearing \textbf{\ru{по}} in front
\end{itemize}

Learning one question word in Russian is nearly learning the set.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{когда}} — \emph{kag-DÁ}, with the first vowel reduced
  \item the three one-word questions in a row — \emph{\ru{что}? \ru{почему}? \ru{когда}?}
  \item the four of the family — \emph{\ru{как}, \ru{что}, \ru{почему}, \ru{когда}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}when.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{когда}}.) What does its first vowel say? (\textbf{A}, because it is unstressed.) How many members of the question family do you now own? (\textbf{Four}.) And one look back: what does the word behind \emph{\ru{сыр}} mean? (\textbf{Sour}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kagdá …, …]{\ru{когда} as a hinge — two things happening at once}

\label{lesson:RU-C19-kogda-soyuz}



\begin{quote}
The last two things on the food list.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{сок}}, a native word with no secure English cousin at all
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{суп}}, borrowed from French, and recent enough that Russians still feel it as a loan
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{другой}}, and the split \emph{\ru{один} … \ru{другой} …}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{очень} \ru{приятно}}, its root meaning \textbf{friend}, and the sentence with no verb in the middle
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the question word, joining}]
\textbf{\ru{что}} asked a question and then hung a clause under a verb without changing a letter. \textbf{\ru{когда}} does exactly the same:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{когда} \ru{я} \ru{читаю}, \ru{я} \ru{думаю}} — \emph{kagdá ya chitáyu, ya dúmayu} — \textbf{when} I read, I think.
\end{itemize}

This time the joining word may go \textbf{first}. Russian is happy to lead with the \emph{when}-half and follow with the main one — and when it does, the comma sits between the two halves rather than before the joining word.

Turn the halves round and the comma travels with the seam:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{когда} \ru{я} \ru{читаю}} — I think \textbf{when} I read.
\end{itemize}

Either order is correct and both mean the same thing. What never changes is that there is a comma at the seam.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{когда} \ru{я} \ru{читаю}, \ru{я} \ru{думаю}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same sentence with the halves the other way round
  \item \emph{Build:} two things you do at the same time, joined with \textbf{\ru{когда}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
May \textbf{\ru{когда}} stand at the front of the whole sentence? (\textbf{Yes} — and then the comma goes at the seam between the halves.) Which other word you own asks a question and joins clauses without changing? (That is \textbf{\ru{что}} — and both of them come off the same ancient question-stem.) And one look back: which food word is a French loan? (That is \textbf{\ru{суп}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zapyatáya]{, — the comma, and the rule with no exceptions}

\label{lesson:RU-W10-zapyataya}



\begin{quote}
The marks you already draw, and two things they were drawn around.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the dot on the line, the single question mark at the end, and the long dash with a space each side
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} …} — and the pattern \emph{\ru{ни} … \ru{ни} …}
  \item \emph{Recall:} all eight of the last letters — \textbf{\ru{а} \ru{о} \ru{г} \ru{х} \ru{ф} \ru{ц} \ru{й} \ru{ю}} — and the one vowel among them that says something else when it is not stressed
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — the hooked-back stroke}
The comma is \textbf{\ru{запятая}}, and the name is a description of the stroke: it means roughly \emph{the one hooked back}. Where \textbf{\ru{точка}} is named for what it looks like — a dot — this one is named for what your hand does.

Start on the writing line, press, and pull the tail down and back to the left. It sits \textbf{below} the line, which is the whole difference from the dot.

\begin{quote}
,
\end{quote}

Draw ten of them in a row and watch that every tail goes the same way.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the rule that has no exceptions}]
English commas are a matter of taste and half of what people argue about is optional. Russian's central comma rule is not optional and has no exceptions:

\textbf{A comma stands at the seam of every subordinate clause.}

Everything that hangs one clause under another takes one — \textbf{\ru{что}}, \textbf{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}, \textbf{\ru{когда}} — every time, in every sentence, whether or not a reader would pause there.

The words that join two equal halves are the other case, and they split:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{и}} — no comma
  \item \textbf{\ru{но}} and \textbf{\ru{а}} — comma, always
\end{itemize}

So one mark, three rules, and only the first of them is absolute. It is worth learning as a single fact because it is the one piece of Russian punctuation an examiner can mark wrong without any argument about style.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ten commas in a row, every tail below the line
  \item \emph{\ru{я} \ru{читаю} \ru{и} \ru{понимаю}} — and put no comma in it
  \item \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{читаю}, \ru{потому} \ru{что} \ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{понимаю}} — and put one in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the joining words you own never takes a comma? (That is \textbf{\ru{и}}.) Which take one always? (\textbf{\ru{но}}, \textbf{\ru{а}}, and everything that hangs a clause underneath — \textbf{\ru{что}}, \textbf{\ru{потому} \ru{что}}, \textbf{\ru{когда}}.) Where does the tail of the comma go? (\textbf{Below the line}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
